title: Salary Negotiation Scripts
summary: Word-for-word scripts for the exact moments that make or break an offer negotiation.

sections.heading: Before You Say Anything: Four Rules That Change the Conversation
sections.body:
Every script in this category assumes you've done three things first: you know your number (a specific figure backed by market data, not a vibe), you know your floor (the number below which you walk), and you're talking to someone who has more practice at this conversation than you do — because it's their job. That last part is why a script helps. Recruiters and hiring managers negotiate offers weekly. You might do it twice in your career. Memorized language closes that gap.

Four things to internalize before you use any script below:

- Never accept or reject a number on the same call it's given to you, even if it's good. "This sounds great — can I take a day to look at the full package and get back to you?" is always available to you, and it costs you nothing. Silence and a pause are more powerful than any clever line.
- Negotiate the whole package, not just base. Base salary is usually the most rigid number in an offer because it hits a pay band that a manager can't override without HR approval. Signing bonus, start date, PTO, remote flexibility, and title are frequently far more flexible because they don't touch that band.
- The first counter is never final. A recruiter who comes back with "let me see what I can do" after your counter is not rejecting you — that's the process working normally. Don't panic-concede on the follow-up call.
- Get the final agreement in writing before you resign your current job or turn down a competing offer. A verbal "yes, we can do $95K" from a hiring manager is not binding. Wait for the revised written offer.

sections.heading: When the Number Is Lower Than You Expected
sections.body:
The instinct when a number lands low is to react immediately — either to accept out of relief that an offer exists at all, or to get visibly frustrated. Neither serves you. The move is to acknowledge warmly, then buy yourself room to respond properly instead of live on the call.

Recruiter: "So the offer is going to come in at $58,000 base, plus our standard benefits package."

You: "Thank you — I really appreciate you walking me through it, and I'm genuinely excited about the team and the role. Can you give me a day or two to look over the full offer in writing before I respond?"

They'll almost always say yes. That gets you off the call without committing to anything. Then, once you have the written offer, you make your actual counter as a separate conversation (see the next script) — ideally over the phone or video, not buried in an email reply, because tone and warmth carry a counter much better than text.

If they push for an immediate reaction on the same call:

You: "I hear you, and I don't want to hold things up — I just want to give this the attention it deserves rather than react on the spot. I'll get back to you by [specific day], I promise it won't drag out."

Giving a specific day, not "soon," is what makes this land as professional rather than evasive.

sections.heading: Countering With a Specific Number (Not Just "Higher")
sections.body:
A counter that isn't anchored to a real number reads as a negotiating tactic with nothing behind it, and it's easy to brush off. A counter anchored to research and your own scope reads as informed, and it's much harder to wave away. Always name a specific figure, and always give a reason that isn't just "I want more."

You: "I've had a chance to look over the offer, and I'm excited about the role. Based on what I'm seeing for [job title] with [X years] of experience in [city/market] — on [Glassdoor / Levels.fyi / your industry's comp survey] — and given that this role also covers [specific added scope, e.g., 'managing the client accounts that used to be split across two people'], I was expecting something closer to $72,000. Is there flexibility to get to that number?"

A shorter version for when you want to keep it tight:

You: "I'd love to make this work. To get there, I'd need base to move to $72,000 — is that something you can work with?"

If they ask you to justify the number further:

You: "Sure — a few data points: [Site] shows the median for this role in this market at $X, a former colleague in a similar role at [type of company] is at $Y, and this role's scope includes [specific responsibility] that wasn't in my last position. $72,000 reflects that."

Never say "I was hoping for more" without a number attached — it invites them to name a small bump and call it done. You naming the number keeps you in control of the anchor.

sections.heading: Using a Competing Offer as Leverage — Without Sounding Like a Threat
sections.body:
A real competing offer is the single strongest negotiating tool you'll have, but it backfires the moment it sounds like an ultimatum or a bluff. The goal is to signal genuine preference for this role while being transparent that there's a real number on the table elsewhere. Never name the other company by name unless you have their explicit permission — you only need to share the number and the timeline.

You: "I want to be upfront with you because I think this role is the better fit for me long-term. I do have another offer in hand at $80,000 with a decision deadline of [date]. I'd genuinely rather join this team — is there room to get closer to that number so I can make this decision easily?"

If they ask you to prove it:

You: "I'm not able to share the offer letter itself, but I'm happy to have my contact there confirm the number and date directly if that's helpful." 

If they can't match it and you still want the job:

You: "I understand you can't get all the way to $80,000. If we could land at $75,000 plus [signing bonus / extra PTO], I'd feel good accepting today."

One caution: only use this script with an offer that actually exists and actually has a deadline. Fabricating one is easy to expose (a simple background-check timeline mismatch, a reference call, or the two companies being in the same small industry can surface it), and a rescinded offer over a lie you can't walk back is a far worse outcome than a smaller number.

sections.heading: Asking for Time Without Sounding Like You're Stalling
sections.body:
Companies expect candidates to ask for time — a request for a few business days is completely normal and almost never counts against you. What makes it land badly is being vague about how much time or why. Always name a specific number of days and a specific reason.

You: "This is exciting news, thank you. I'd like to take a couple of days to review the full offer in detail and talk it through with my [partner/family] before I give you my answer — would [specific date, 2-3 business days out] work for getting back to you?"

If they push for a faster answer than you're comfortable with:

You: "I completely understand you're working against a timeline. I can commit to getting back to you by [move it up slightly, e.g., end of day Wednesday instead of Friday] — will that work on your end?"

If you're waiting specifically because of a competing process:

You: "I'm very interested in this role and want to give you a real answer, not a placeholder. I do have another process wrapping up on [date] — could I get back to you the day after that, on [date]?"

The underlying principle: silence with no timeline reads as hesitation about the job. Silence with a specific date attached reads as someone being thorough. The date is what makes the difference.

sections.heading: When Base Won't Move: Asking for a Signing Bonus
sections.body:
Base salary often can't move because it's tied to a pay band or internal equity with existing employees on the team — moving it requires sign-off from more people than a signing bonus does. A signing bonus is frequently a one-time, discretionary line item the hiring manager can approve directly, which makes it the highest-leverage ask once you hear "I really can't move base any further."

You: "I understand base is locked in at $X — I appreciate you being straight with me about that. Would there be flexibility on a signing bonus to help bridge the gap? Something in the range of $5,000 would get me comfortable saying yes today."

If you're leaving money on the table elsewhere (unvested equity, a bonus you'd miss by leaving mid-cycle):

You: "Part of what makes this a harder decision is that I'd be walking away from a bonus of about $X at my current company that pays out in [month]. A signing bonus in that range would make the timing work for me."

If they counter with a smaller number:

You: "I appreciate you finding room there. Could we meet at $3,500? That would get me to a yes."

Always ask explicitly whether the signing bonus has a clawback clause (a requirement to repay it if you leave within a certain window) and get the window in writing — most do, and it's a normal, fair term, but you want to know it going in rather than discover it later.

sections.heading: Negotiating More Paid Time Off
sections.body:
PTO is one of the easiest asks in this entire list because it costs the company far less than the equivalent value in salary, and most PTO policies have an unofficial "senior hire" exception that recruiters can grant without much friction — but only if you ask directly instead of hoping it's included.

You: "One thing that matters to me is PTO — I currently have [X weeks] and would like to stay close to that rather than reset to a standard first-year allotment. Is there flexibility to start me at [Y weeks] instead of the standard [Z]?"

If they say PTO policy is fixed for all new hires regardless of level:

You: "That's understandable if it's a hard policy. Would it be possible to structure it as an additional week granted at hire rather than changing the standard policy itself, so it doesn't set a different precedent?"

A version for when you're negotiating this alongside salary, not instead of it:

You: "I'd be comfortable accepting the base salary as offered if we could add one extra week of PTO on top of the standard allotment — does that work?"

Framing it as "an additional week granted to me" rather than "changing your PTO policy" is what usually gets this approved quickly — it doesn't require them to justify a policy exception to anyone else on the team.

sections.heading: Negotiating Remote or Hybrid Flexibility
sections.body:
Remote and hybrid asks land very differently depending on whether you're asking for a blanket policy exception or a specific, bounded arrangement. "Can I work remote" is a policy question that often has to go up a chain. "Can I work from home on Mondays and Fridays" is a scheduling question a direct manager can usually just say yes to.

You: "I saw the role is listed as hybrid, three days in office. Would it be possible to do two days in office instead, with Mondays and Fridays remote? I'm most productive doing focused work from home and value the in-person time midweek for collaboration."

If the role is fully in-office and you're asking for an exception:

You: "I understand the team works in-office. Given [specific reason — a commute distance, a caregiving schedule], would you be open to a trial period of one remote day a week, revisited after 90 days based on how it's working for the team?"

Proposing a defined trial period, rather than asking for a permanent change up front, is usually the difference between a quick yes and a request that has to escalate — it gives the manager a low-risk way to say yes without committing to anything open-ended. If they agree, ask for the specific arrangement (days, review date) to be noted in the offer letter or a follow-up email, not left as a verbal understanding.

sections.heading: Negotiating Your Title
sections.body:
Title negotiations matter more than they get credit for — a title affects how you're perceived internally from day one, and it follows you to your next job search on your resume and LinkedIn regardless of what the pay was. It's also frequently the cheapest thing in the entire offer for a company to change, since it usually doesn't touch a pay band or headcount budget at all.

You: "I noticed the offer has the title as [Associate Marketing Manager]. Given that I'd be coming in with [X years] of directly relevant experience and managing [specific scope, e.g., 'the same paid social budget I ran at my last company'], would it be possible to bring the title in as [Marketing Manager] instead?"

If they say title is tied strictly to internal leveling:

You: "That makes sense if it's tied to a formal level. Is there a path to revisit the title at the [6-month / annual] review if I'm hitting the scope we're discussing today? I'd want that noted somewhere so it's not just a verbal understanding."

A version when you're using title as the trade for a base number that won't move:

You: "If base is firm at $X, I'd be comfortable there if we could adjust the title to [Senior Analyst] rather than [Analyst] — the scope of the role supports it, and it matters for how this shows up on my resume going forward."

Always get any agreed title change into the written offer letter itself, not just an email aside — it's the document you'll point to at review time.

sections.heading: "What's Your Current Salary?" — Answering Without Anchoring Yourself Low
sections.body:
This question is designed to give the other side a ceiling to negotiate down from, and in a growing number of states and cities it's actually illegal for an employer to ask directly — but plenty still ask anyway, out of habit or because they're not in one of those jurisdictions. Either way, the goal is the same: redirect to the number you want for the new role without lying and without volunteering the exact figure.

Interviewer: "What are you currently making?"

You: "I'd rather focus on what this role is worth and what I'm looking for going forward, since I'm making a career move rather than a lateral shift. Based on my research and the scope of this position, I'm targeting $75,000 to $80,000 — does that align with the budget for this role?"

If they push again for the specific current number:

You: "I understand you're trying to make sure we're in the same range — I'd prefer to keep the focus on the new role's value rather than my current comp, which honestly isn't a great benchmark since [it was set two years ago / it included equity that doesn't apply here / the scope is different]. What's the budgeted range for this position?"

If you're in a state where the employer is legally barred from asking (check your state and city — this list has expanded quickly):

You: "I believe [state] restricts employers from asking about salary history, so I'd rather not share that — but I'm glad to tell you my target range for this role, which is $X to $Y."

Said warmly and without hesitation, none of these come across as evasive — they come across as someone who knows how to advocate for themselves, which is itself a mark in your favor.
